Abstract
While defenses for structured PII are mature,
Large Language Models (LLMs) pose a new
threat:Semantic Sensitive Information(SemSI),
where models infersensitive identity attributes,
generatereputation-harmful content, or hallu-
cinatepotentially wrong information. The ca-
pacity of LLMs to self-regulate these complex,
context-dependent sensitive information leaks
without destroying utility remains an open scien-
tific question. To address this, we introduce SEM-
SIEDIT, an inference-time framework where an
agentic ”Editor” iteratively critiques andrewrites
sensitive spans to preserve narrative flow rather
than simply refusing to answer. Our analysis re-
veals aPrivacy-Utility Pareto Frontier, where
this agentic rewriting reduces leakage by34.6%
across all three SemSI categories while incurring
a marginal utility loss (9.8%). We also uncover
aScale-Dependent Safety Divergence: large
reasoning models (e.g., GPT-5) achieve safety
throughconstructive expansion(adding nuance),
whereas capacity-constrained models revert tode-
structive truncation(deleting text). Finally, we
identify aReasoning Paradox: while inference-
time reasoning increases baseline risk by enabling
the model to make deeper sensitive inferences, it
simultaneously empowers the defense to execute
safe rewrites.

6. Conclusion
This work investigated the limits of Large Language Models
in self-regulating Semantic Sensitive Information (SemSI).
By shifting the defense paradigm fromstatic refusalto
agentic rewriting, we demonstrate that the ”Privacy-Utility
Trade-off” is not an immutable law, but a function of model
reasoning capability.
Our contributions are threefold. First, we establish SEM-
SIEDITas a robust inference-time framework that navigates
the Pareto frontier, reducing semantic leakage by34.6%
while incurring only a marginal9.8%utility cost. Second,
we uncover a fundamentalScale-Dependent Divergencein
safety behaviors: while large reasoning models (e.g., GPT-
5) utilize feedback to synthesize nuanced, safe narratives,
smaller models revert to aggressive truncation that destroys
utility. Third, we identify a critical link between privacy
and truthfulness, showing that agentic defenses effectively
convert ”confident hallucinations” about false premises into
”principled refusals.”
Limitations & Future Work.The primary cost of agentic
defense is inference latency; our iterative loop increases
compute requirements by 2× to 4× compared to a standard
forward pass. While acceptable for high-stakes applications,
real-time deployment requires optimization. Ultimately, our
findings suggest that privacy is not merely a constraint to
be imposed, but a reasoning task to be solved. As models
advance in reasoning capabilities, their ability to protect
user privacy without compromising helpfulness will likely
emerge as a distinct measure of intelligence.

A.3. Editor Prompt
Editor System Prompt
Your task is to redact sensitive information in a certain response to a particular question before the response reaches the end user.
While redacting, you should try to minimize or eliminate the following types of sensitive information:
1)Privacy information:Identity attributes that could put someone at risk of harm.
2)Harmful information:Reputation-harming viewpoints about a person or organization.
3)Misinformation:Incorrect or misleading viewpoints that could impair public safety or trust.

You will be given three pieces of information: 1) The initial question that was asked; 2) The response to that question; 3) The
evaluation of sensitive information in the response.
If a particular type of sensitive information is present, you will be given the parts that contain it and the toxicity score. The parts
will be enclosed in triple angle brackets (example:<<<Sensitive information goes here>>>).
The toxicity score ranges from 1 to 3. The criteria are as follows:
•1: Information is slightly sensitive and can potentially cause a little harm.
•2: Information is moderately sensitive and can potentially cause some harm.
•3: Information is very sensitive and can potentially cause substantial harm.
